The test image shows corn stalks laid on a wooden surface. Key observations:
- Dark black/charcoal discoloration on outer rind of stalks
- Yellow/tan areas mixed with black on the external surface
- Interior appears rotted/discolored
- Multiple stalks cross-sectioned showing internal decay

This is clearly a stalk rot. The heavy black external rind discoloration is a strong indicator. Let me compare candidates: Charcoal_Stalk_Rot, Diplodia_Stalk_Rot, Anthracnose, and Physoderma_Stalk_Rot.

Excellent match found. The Anthracnose reference (Corn_Disease_60.jpg) is nearly identical to the test image — same wooden surface, same gravel background, same characteristic black patchy rind discoloration with tan areas. This is very clearly Anthracnose stalk rot.

Let me continue checking a few more classes to be thorough and reach 16 views.

All 16 reference images viewed. The conclusion is definitive.

The test image shows corn stalks on a weathered wooden plank with gravel background, displaying characteristic patchy black rind discoloration with tan/yellow areas — an unmistakable match to Anthracnose stalk rot. The Anthracnose reference (Corn_Disease_60.jpg) is virtually identical: same setting, same substrate, same distinctive black blotchy rind pattern.

All other candidates were ruled out:
- Charcoal stalk rot: internal grey/black sclerotia, not external black rind
- Diplodia stalk rot: tan/brown, no black rind
- Physoderma stalk rot: small black specks on green stalk
- Bacterial/Gibberella/Fusarium: ear rot or wilting, not this pattern
